tip: Doubling καλά (kala = well) flips it to 'barely': πριν καλά καλά ξημερώσει (prin kala kala ximerosi) = before day had even properly broken.
όμως (omos = but/however) floats: it can open the clause – όμως εκείνος ήξερε (omos ekinos ixere = but he knew) – or slide in second: εκείνος όμως (ekinos omos).
For 'had done', Greek uses είχε (ihe = had) plus a fixed verb form: είχε ήδη αποφασίσει (ihe idi apofasisi = had already decided). αποφασίσει never changes for person.
κι ας (ki as) is literally 'and let' – Greek concedes by letting: κι ας είχαν σκορπίσει (ki as ihan skorpisi) = even though they'd scattered.
κολλάω (kollao) literally means 'stick', so κάτι δεν κόλλαγε (kati den kollage = something didn't stick) is Greek for 'something didn't add up'.
μα (ma) is an everyday 'but' alongside αλλά (alla), often with a touch of emphasis: όχι με ρολόγια μα με προσευχές (ohi me rologia ma me prosefhes = not by clocks but by prayers).
λάδι (ladi) is literally 'oil': η θάλασσα ήταν λάδι (i thalassa itan ladi = the sea was oil). Where English sees glass in a calm sea, Greek sees oil.
θα μπορούσε να υποστηριχθεί (tha borouse na ypostirihthi = it could be argued) has no 'it' – Greek drops the dummy subject English must supply.
δεδομένου ότι (dedomenou oti = given that) is a frozen leftover: the -ου (-ou) ending comes from an old 'this being given' construction and never changes form.
συνεπώς (synepos = therefore) is the lighter way to draw a consequence; κατά συνέπεια (kata synepia) says the same thing with more formal weight.
ενδεχομένως (endehomenos = possibly) can put the main verb in the να (na) form: να μας εμποδίζει (na mas embodizi = it may prevent us). The doubt shows on the verb itself.
προκειμένου να (prokimenou na) is the formal twin of everyday για να (ya na = in order to): προκειμένου να διασφαλιστεί (prokimenou na diasfalisti = so as to ensure) belongs in reports, not chat.
καταρχήν (katarhin) = in principle; καταρχάς (katarhas) = first of all – even native speakers swap them. Here καταρχήν (katarhin) opens a matter of principle, not a list.
λαμβανομένων υπόψη (lamvanomenon ypopsi = taking into account) changes its ending to match των περιορισμών (ton periorismon = the limits). Everyday Greek uses λαμβάνοντας (lamvanontas) instead.
πρίσμα (prisma) is literally 'prism': υπό αυτό το πρίσμα (ypo afto to prisma = under this prism) is how Greek says 'seen in this light'.
